Lessons.Title: Measure in Halves of an Inch
ExplanationParagraphs: Original Illustrative Mathematics 2021 Grade 3 Unit 6 Lesson 1 opens a new measurement unit under CCSS 3.MD.B.4. The 2021 LOCAL teacher lesson and preparation HTML on Our-CS were compared to the original 3-PAGE Student Task Statements PDF read from the owner-device file. PDF page 1 contains the source warm-up 'What Do You Know About Inches?' (one open oral prompt); PDF page 2 contains 1.1 Measure Around the Room (one open task with an object/length-in-inches table); PDF page 3 contains 1.2 Partition Inches into Halves (TWO numbered directions and an object/length-in-inches table). These are original modelling tasks and have no preprinted fixed object measurements.

Warm-up (10 minutes): Ask 'What do you know about inches?' Record observations. Inches are units of length on a ruler; numbers refer to positions at increasing distances from zero. In grade 2 students measured whole inches; now objects can end between consecutive whole-inch ticks. Students may supply several valid facts or examples. This is a discussion prompt, NOT an automatic numerical question.

Activity 1 Measure Around the Room (15 minutes): give each pupil an INCH ruler copied from the source blackline-master sheet (teacher prep says five rulers per page). Students work in PAIRS but EACH student should choose THREE objects and measure their lengths using whole-inch tick marks. Record object name and measured length in inches in the PDF's two-column table. Teacher prompts when an endpoint falls between whole-inch marks: near which whole mark? Don't invent lengths of student-chosen shoes, pencils, notebooks or classroom furniture. The correct answer depends on actual measured object, ruler zero alignment, unit and choice of nearest whole/estimate.

Activity 2 Partition Inches into Halves (20 minutes): each partner group reuses TWO rulers from Activity1, then selects ONE ruler to add a mark EXACTLY halfway between each consecutive pair of whole-inch marks. Preserve the OTHER ruler with whole-inch marks only so students can compare accuracy. The teacher asks why splitting 0–1,1–2,2–3, etc into two equal intervals improves the precision of measurements. A half-inch is always 1/2 of the SAME one-inch unit, not half the entire printed ruler.

Student PDF page 3 numbered step (1): work with a partner and partition EVERY inch on ONE ruler into half inches. Numbered step (2): use that marked ruler to measure actual objects around the room and record object name with measured length in inches. Original launch says EACH partner again measures THREE objects and reports lengths to the NEAREST HALF INCH; if a physical object ends between half-inch ticks, use nearest mark and justify. These are student-generated measurements. Teachers check zero alignment, even half intervals, ruler reuse, consistent units and realistic estimate/rounding.

Original teacher synthesis (10 minutes): rulers act like number lines. Both label distances increasing to the right, and both can be partitioned into fractions. A length of N half-inch intervals can be represented as N/2 inches, a whole plus half, or a mixed number. Source example 9/2 inches =4 1/2 inches. Also 7/2=3 1/2, and 13/2=6 1/2 as independent extensions; these examples are NOT publisher fixed questions. The 2021 lesson explicitly INTRODUCES the word 'mixed numbers' here: whole number and fraction less than 1. An improper half-inch length and a mixed number name the SAME location on ruler.

Teacher differentiation: MLR2 Collect and Display word choices such as 'seven half inches', 'seven halves of an inch', 'between 2 and 3 inches' and 'six and a half inches'. Student with attention/organization needs may receive chunked measurement tasks. Source original hand/ruler/pencil photograph was only described through source file and no publisher artwork is embedded. The 2021 blackline master cut-out ruler file and restricted publisher Cool-down 'Length in Half Inches' were NOT independently inspected. Source measured student object lengths are teacher-assessed; do not claim Stage D, publisher assessment parity, live app persistence or executed tests.

KeyConcepts.Title: The inch ruler as number line
KeyConcepts.Definition: Inches are equal units of length. Each tick labels the distance from the ruler's zero point.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Align one end of the object with 0; read at the other endpoint.
KeyConcepts.Example: An object ending halfway between 4 and 5 is near 4 1/2 inches.

KeyConcepts.Title: Partition every whole inch into halves
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each 1-inch interval can be divided into two equal parts by a single center mark.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Mark k+1/2 between integer inch positions k and k+1.

KeyConcepts.Title: Nearest half-inch measurement
KeyConcepts.Definition: Read/estimate the closest half-inch tick for a physical endpoint; there may be a small rounding difference.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Reported inches are multiples of 1/2 (n/2), with distance measured from zero.

KeyConcepts.Title: Mixed numbers
KeyConcepts.Definition: Whole part plus fractional part less than one, like 4 1/2.

WorkedExamples.Title: Choose an object and measure
WorkedExamples.Question: A pupil measures a notebook with an inch-only ruler. What must they record?
WorkedExamples.Method: Line up the ruler at zero and find the object's end.
Steps: Choose a real object and write its name.
Align one end to the zero tick.
Read or approximate the other end in inches.
Record observation; teacher checks actual object/ruler.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No universal number; measurement is student-specific
WorkedExamples.Check: 3 different objects per student in Activity1.

WorkedExamples.Title: Build a half-inch ruler
WorkedExamples.Question: Where does the new mark go between 3 and 4 inches?
WorkedExamples.Method: Divide the original one-inch interval into two equal lengths.
Steps: Locate the point halfway between them.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both half-inch spaces must be equal.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find nearest half-inch
WorkedExamples.Question: If an object ends closest to the half-inch mark between 2 and 3, what length is recorded?
WorkedExamples.Method: Read the nearest tick after ruler zero.
WorkedExamples.Check: This is an independently authored example, NOT a source pupil's actual object.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source mixed-number synthesis
WorkedExamples.Question: Explain 9/2 and 4 1/2 as ruler measurements.
WorkedExamples.Method: Group nine halves into four whole inches and one additional half.
Steps: Every two halves make one inch.
Nine halves make4 inches plus1/2 inch.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both names refer to same tick.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Start measuring at the physical ruler edge instead of the zero tick.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The physical margin may not be zero, causing offset error.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Align the object with the marked zero.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Divide the ruler's whole length into two rather than EACH individual inch.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: That creates one half-ruler, not half-inch intervals.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assign a fixed textbook answer to the object-measurement tables.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original student tables are blank and pupils freely choose their classroom objects.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Record actual objects and evidence; teacher inspects lengths.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Equate improper fractions with a larger measurement than mixed numbers.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count half-inch intervals and convert whole pairs.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Mark every half-inch correctly but measure an object with an unpartitioned ruler.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Activity 2 explicitly requires the marked ruler to be used.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep one old whole-inch ruler for contrast, and use partitioned ruler to measure.

SummaryPoints: Original 2021 student PDF verified:3 pages; warm-up what know about inches; Activity1 3 real objects per pupil with inch ruler and table; Activity2 two numbered actions and 3 further real objects per pupil measured to nearest half-inch.
Two rulers per pair: partition EVERY whole inch on one ruler, retain the other whole-inch ruler.
Zero alignment, midpoint placement and real measurement evidence are essential; arbitrary fixed numeric assessment would be false source parity.
Source synthesis introduces mixed numbers with9/2=4 1/2 and explains ruler/number-line connection.
Original blackline master, publisher hand-ruler photograph parity and gated Cool-down not verified; authored tests and Stage D unrun.
